#### Why this design needs to retract a negative, and what it still loses

**The question.** Join a click stream and an impression stream for ad attribution. The join must buffer each side until both watermarks pass, and a late row arriving afterwards must retract and correct the earlier attribution.

**The pipeline:** click stream + impression stream → windowed join (buffer + watermark) → retraction emitter → attribution store.

**The retraction emitter is not optional**, and its hard requirement is unusual: it must be able to retract a **negative**. Click 0 publishes "matched no impression" after event 5, and impression 7 later proves that wrong. Updating a number is easy; un-publishing an absence usually needs an explicit tombstone in the store.

**And here is what the store actually ends up with.** Of the 5 true matches in the data: **1 published correctly first time** (20%), **2 published after a retraction**, **2 never published** (40%) — from 2 clicks whose watermark bound the minimum never reaches.

The never-published group is the one that matters commercially, and the pipeline does not report it. An absent attribution looks exactly like a click that genuinely matched nothing.

**Two settings, and neither fixes the biggest loss.** Widening the join window adds candidate pairs *and* buffer, linearly. Raising allowed lateness holds buffered rows longer so late matches can emit. Neither touches the 2 clicks blocked by the minimum watermark — only an idleness timeout on the slower input does, and that trades away exactly the correctness the minimum rule was protecting.

#### When to ship this, and the four things it does not settle

**Ship it when the attribution consumer tolerates corrections**, including the withdrawal of a no-match, and when an under-count is survivable. For reporting that is usually fine; for payouts it is not.

**Instrument the undelivered case before launch.** Compute, from the retained streams, what the attribution *should* have been and compare. Nothing in the pipeline will tell you about the 2 missing matches.

**Decide the idleness policy deliberately.** It is the only lever on the never-emitted matches, and it is a correctness trade dressed as a timeout value.

**What this design does NOT settle — four gaps:**

1. **2 of the 5 true matches are never published and nothing reports it.** Absence of an attribution is indistinguishable from a genuine non-match, so this gap is invisible from inside the system.
2. **The store must retract a negative result.** "Click 0 matched nothing" is published and later false — a harder store requirement than revising a value.
3. **Buffer is arrival rate × 60s per side**, 5 rows on this stream, and both tuning knobs scale it linearly. Nothing here bounds it at a real traffic rate.
4. **One click matches 2 impressions**, so the join's output can exceed either input and somebody must decide which impression gets the credit. First touch, last touch or split is a business decision this design cannot make — and it cannot ship without one.

<summary><b>Step 1 of 4</b> — the pipeline, and the stage that only this design needs</summary>

<img src="../diagrams/anim/ch09-system/frames/step-01.svg" alt="Step 1: the pipeline, and the stage that only this design needs" width="1040">

The hard requirement in this design is retracting a **negative**. "Click 0 matched no impression" is published as a fact and later becomes false, so the attribution store needs to express "forget what I said about this click" — which is harder than updating a number, and worth discovering at design time.

</details>
<details>
<summary><b>Step 2 of 4</b> — the attribution outcome, counted honestly</summary>

<img src="../diagrams/anim/ch09-system/frames/step-02.svg" alt="Step 2: the attribution outcome, counted honestly" width="1040">

This is the number an attribution design has to put in front of someone: 1 of 5 matches right the first time, 2 corrected later, 2 never delivered. The last group is silent — the pipeline does not report a missing attribution, so the only way to know is to compute what it should have been, which is what this generator does.

</details>
<details>
<summary><b>Step 3 of 4</b> — the two settings, and what each one actually fixes</summary>

<img src="../diagrams/anim/ch09-system/frames/step-03.svg" alt="Step 3: the two settings, and what each one actually fixes" width="1040">

Both knobs grow the state and neither touches the biggest loss. The 2 undelivered matches are blocked by the minimum watermark, and the only thing that unblocks them is declaring the slower input idle — which is exactly the correctness the minimum rule was protecting. That trade is a product decision presented as a config value.

</details>
<details>
<summary><b>Step 4 of 4</b> — and what this design does NOT settle</summary>

<img src="../diagrams/anim/ch09-system/frames/step-04.svg" alt="Step 4: and what this design does NOT settle" width="1040">

The fourth gap is the one that is a business question rather than an engineering one: one click matches 2 impressions, so the join emits more rows than it received and somebody has to decide which impression gets the credit. Nothing about windows, watermarks or retractions answers that — but the design cannot ship without it being answered.

</details>
